newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA BUSINESS VOICES CONCERN TO LABOUR MINISTER.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA BUSINESS VOICES CONCERN TO LABOUR MINISTER.

text.p: South African business leaders met Labour Minister Tito Mboweni on Thursday to express their concerns that labour legislation now being formulated should not sabotage a planned jobs summit later this year.

"What we're trying to say is, it should be part of a bigger plan and everything should be coordinated within that plan and not happening at random," Leslie Boyd of Business South Africa told a news conference after the 90-minute meeting.

"Jobs are the biggest challenge this country has and we are fully behind the government in moving forward with the job summit but we don't want to have our hands tied at that summit by decisions that we might take at this point in time," he said.
The labour ministry last month announced plans for a Presidential Jobs Summit to be held later this year.

Boyd said the request for a meeting with Mboweni was not linked to trade union strike threats over the controversial Basic Conditions of Employment Bill, which earlier this week sparked a one-day national work stoppage.
The bill is due to be finalised this year and implemented next year.
Mboweni said the view of the meeting was that there should be "some relationship between the bill and the objectives, and possible outcomes, of the job summit".

"So if for example the summit felt certain provisions of the bill were in contradiction to the objectives of the summit, what do we need to do to avoid anything that may be a negative outcome in terms of job creation," he said.

"Then, probably, one could arrive at a number of options which say, there's a relationship, so we need to have the number of hours dealt with in this manner, the overtime rate dealt with in this manner, the parental rights issue dealt with in this maner," Mboweni said.
He said the the Congress of South African Trade Unions' strike threat was not discussed, but he added:

"I will in the next couple of weeks be requesting a meeting with leaders of the trade union movement. We need to discuss what is to be done in resolving the difficulties in the Nedlac process, to ensure we bring talking back into the process."

Business, government and labour have been negotiating in the National Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) since April last year with a view to finding consensus on the employment bill but talks stalled last month.
The 1.9 million member Cosatu federation on Monday threatened fresh strike action if business failed to present revised proposals on the bill within fourteen days.
Mboweni said he wanted to draw up an overall approach to deal with labour issues. Both Mboweni and Boyd described Thursday's meeting as constructive.
